memory_update.text: For Consumer, prioritize infrastructure nodes over consumer-facing brands: retailer-supplier EDI networks, compliance/traceability data, upstream inventory buffers, sourcing diversification, logistics messaging, private-label capacity, formulation inputs, packaging, restaurant/hospitality operating software, specialty distribution, and repair/remodel channels.
Highest initial bottleneck score belongs to retailer-supplier transaction networks because switching costs appear operational and embedded in integrations, compliance logic, and trading-partner maps.
Grocery traceability and supplier-compliance data should remain a top low-attention bottleneck candidate, especially if retailer mandates or food-safety regulation force supplier onboarding.

Retail inventory visibility and upstream buffer capacity are emerging bottleneck nodes as store-centric fulfillment and cautious inventory buying require better forecasting, receive-center capacity, and responsive suppliers.
Tariff volatility and sourcing-country risk can catalyze investment in direct sourcing infrastructure, trade compliance, cross-border logistics software, and multi-country supplier relationships.
Retailer capex into receive centers, food distribution centers, and fulfillment infrastructure can shift value upstream toward forecasting, supplier connectivity, and replenishment systems.

Private-label growth remains a possible Consumer catalyst, but it should be verified through manufacturer utilization, customer concentration, contract structure, pricing pass-through, and gross-margin progression rather than assumed from retailer shelf-power narratives.

Need primary-source verification for SPSC trading-partner count, recurring revenue percentage, net retention, customer concentration, tariff-related sales-cycle impact, and retailer/supplier dependency.

Need primary-source verification for TRAK supplier-count growth, FSMA 204 sensitivity, named retailer mandates, customer concentration, retention, and conversion of supplier onboarding into durable recurring revenue.
Need segment-level exposure checks for DSGX, AGYS, PAR, CHEF, SXT, SLGN, THS, GFF, FBIN, and MGPI before advancing any company-level conclusion beyond hypothesis.

summary: Initial Layer 2A industry-chain map for the broad Consumer theme. The map deliberately de-emphasizes high-attention consumer brands and mega-cap retailers, and instead focuses on the hidden infrastructure that allows consumer demand to convert into revenue: retailer-supplier transaction networks, grocery/food compliance data, private-label manufacturing, packaging and formulation inputs, hospitality/restaurant operating software, specialty distribution, and home-improvement repair/remodel channels. The highest bottleneck candidates are not the most visible brands, but the nodes with operational switching costs, regulatory or customer-certification gates, route density, retailer mandates, or embedded workflow dependence.

supply_chain_map.node: Retailer-supplier transaction network / EDI compliance layer
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Retailers, suppliers, and brands depend on order, invoice, advance-shipping-notice, routing-guide, and compliance-message connectivity. The bottleneck may sit in long-lived trading-partner maps and retailer-specific integrations rather than in visible storefront demand.

supply_chain_map.node: Grocery and food-retail traceability / supplier compliance data
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Food retailers and suppliers increasingly need auditable supplier documentation, traceability, and compliance workflows. If retailer mandates and regulatory deadlines force onboarding, a small compliance network can become a hidden toll road.

supply_chain_map.node: Retail inventory visibility, forecasting, and upstream buffer capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Store-centric fulfillment and cautious inventory buying increase dependence on accurate out-of-stock detection, demand forecasting, upstream receive centers, and supplier responsiveness. The bottleneck shifts from stores to upstream buffers and replenishment agility.

supply_chain_map.node: Private-label food manufacturing and retailer-controlled brand capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Retailers can use shelf power and value positioning to expand private-label penetration, but this requires reliable manufacturers, formulation capability, category-specific capacity, and pass-through pricing discipline.

supply_chain_map.node: Consumer formulation inputs: colors, flavors, ingredients, specialty additives
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Food, beverage, personal-care, and household-products companies rely on qualified ingredients and formulation partners. Customer qualification, regulatory documentation, and reformulation complexity can create switching friction.

supply_chain_map.node: Rigid packaging, closures, dispensing systems, and food/household packaging
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Packaging can look commodity-like, but food and household customers often need qualified plants, line compatibility, proximity, continuity of supply, and pass-through contracts. This can hide modest bottleneck value inside industrial packaging labels.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant and QSR operating systems: POS, loyalty, ordering, back office
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Restaurants and franchise operators increasingly depend on embedded software for ordering, payments, loyalty, kitchen workflow, and back-office controls. Switching costs may come from implementation depth and workflow lock-in.

supply_chain_map.node: Hospitality property and venue operating software
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Hotels, resorts, casinos, and managed venues require property-management, payments, POS, booking, and operational workflow systems. This node is exposed to consumer travel demand but has more infrastructure-like characteristics than hotel brands.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty foodservice distribution and independent restaurant procurement
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Specialty restaurants need broad SKUs, supplier relationships, route density, and reliable delivery. The visible demand driver is restaurant traffic, but the hidden node is distribution density and procurement breadth.

supply_chain_map.node: Cross-border retail logistics and trade-compliance messaging
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Tariff volatility, sourcing diversification, customs complexity, and omnichannel fulfillment increase dependence on logistics networks and trade-compliance software. Consumer exposure is often buried inside logistics rather than labeled as retail.

supply_chain_map.node: Direct sourcing offices, vendor diversification, and country-of-origin flexibility
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Retailers with long-built sourcing offices and supplier relationships can respond to tariff or country-risk shocks better than brands dependent on one sourcing geography. The chokepoint is not a single supplier, but sourcing optionality built over years.

supply_chain_map.node: Home-improvement repair/remodel channel and pro/retail distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Housing-linked consumer demand can flow through repair/remodel categories even when new construction is weak. Channel concentration at major home-improvement retailers and pro distributors makes customer access and category share important.

supply_chain_map.node: Beverage alcohol contract production, barrel inventory, and specialty spirits supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Distilled spirits supply can be constrained by aging inventory, contract relationships, and brand/contract mix. The node is cyclical and evidence-sensitive, but hidden value may exist if inventory quality and customer stickiness are underappreciated.
